Execrable
ĕk´sē-kra-bl
adj. (deserving to be cursed; accursed; detestable)
Latin execrabilis, from ex- and sacer, sacred — to execrate is to devote out of the sacred, to place under a curse. The AV's word is accursed, and the Greek is anathema.

Biblical Definition

An execrable thing is one placed under a curse. Paul pronounces it on a doctrine, twice, including against himself: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8), and on a settled disposition: “If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema” (1Co 16:22). Achan's theft made a whole camp accursed: “neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed from among you” (Jos 7:12). The Law placed the hanged man under it: “he that is hanged is accursed of God” (Deu 21:23). And that is where the doctrine turns: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines execrable as deserving to be cursed; very hateful; detestable; abominable; and execrate as to curse, to denounce evil against.

expand to see more

EXECRABLE, a. Deserving to be cursed; very hateful; detestable; abominable.

EXECRATE, v.t. To curse; to denounce evil against, or to imprecate evil on; to abominate; to abhor.

EXECRATION, n. The act of cursing; a curse pronounced; imprecation of evil.

Key Scripture

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

1Co 16:22 — "If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha."

Jos 7:12 — "Therefore the children of Israel could not stand before their enemies, but turned their backs before their enemies, because they were accursed: neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed from among you."

Deu 21:23 — "His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled, which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance."

Gal 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

Modern Corruption

The anathema is used as a weapon in disputes it was never meant for, and the one place it lands hardest is on Christ.

expand to see more

Galatians 1:8 is the strongest sentence in the New Testament and the church has repeatedly borrowed its force for arguments Paul never had in mind. What is under the curse there is another gospel — specifically, the addition of circumcision to faith as a condition of acceptance with God. Not a difference over church order, or eschatology, or a translation, or a hundred things over which anathemas have since been pronounced. The verse's own guard is the clause including the apostle and an angel: a man who invokes it must be prepared to stand under the same standard, and the willingness to do that is rare among people who quote it.

Joshua 7 shows how seriously the Old Testament takes the category and why. The accursed thing in Achan's tent was not merely his private sin; it made the entire camp accursed, so that Israel could not stand before its enemies until it was dealt with. That is the doctrine of corporate holiness in its hardest form, and it lies behind the New Testament's instruction to put away from among yourselves that wicked person. A church that cannot bring itself to deal with a known and unrepented evil has not been merciful; it has left the thing in the camp.

Then Galatians 3:13 turns the whole doctrine round, and it does so by quoting Deuteronomy 21:23. Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. The execrable thing on the hill outside the city was the Son of God, placed under the curse by law and by design, so that those who were under it might be bought out. Every anathema in the Bible is answered there, and no Christian may pronounce one without remembering who took the last one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anathema (G331), a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; katara (G2671), a curse; Hebrew cherem (H2764), a devoted thing; qelalah (H7045), a curse.

expand to see more

Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8–9, 1 Corinthians 16:22, Romans 9:3.

Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted or accursed thing; Joshua 6:17–18, 7:1, 7:11–13.

Greek katara (G2671) — curse; Galatians 3:10, 3:13, Hebrews 6:8, James 3:10.

Usage

"“Though we, or an angel from heaven” — and he includes himself."

"“Except ye destroy the accursed from among you” — it was in the camp."

"“Being made a curse for us” — where every anathema is answered."
